## Shared function for questions

```{r}
# function to calculate the stationary state probabilities
stationary <- function(Gamma) {
  k <- nrow(Gamma)

  # set up the equations for delta Gamma = delta
  A <- t(Gamma) - diag(k)

  # replace one equation so the probabilities sum to 1
  A[k, ] <- 1
  b <- c(rep(0, k - 1), 1)

  # solve for the stationary probabilities
  as.numeric(solve(A, b))
}

# function to simulate the hidden state sequence
simulate_states <- function(n, Gamma, delta) {
  states <- integer(n)

  # sample the first state using the initial probabilities
  states[1] <- sample.int(nrow(Gamma), 1, prob = delta)

  # sample each next state using the previous state's transition row
  if (n > 1) {
    for (t in 2:n) {
      states[t] <- sample.int(
        nrow(Gamma), 1,
        prob = Gamma[states[t - 1], ]
      )
    }
  }

  states
}

# function for the forward algorithm
# each row of emission gives the observation likelihood under each state
forward_hmm <- function(emission, Gamma, delta) {
  n <- nrow(emission)
  k <- ncol(emission)

  # storage for the filtered state probabilities
  filtered <- matrix(NA_real_, n, k)
  loglik <- 0
  prob <- delta

  for (t in seq_len(n)) {

    # predict the current state probabilities from the previous step
    if (t > 1) prob <- drop(prob %*% Gamma)

    # combine the state probabilities with the observation likelihoods
    weight <- prob * emission[t, ]
    scale <- sum(weight)

    # stop if the normalising value is zero or not finite
    if (!is.finite(scale) || scale <= 0) {
      return(list(loglik = -Inf, filtered = filtered))
    }

    # normalise so the updated probabilities sum to 1
    prob <- weight / scale
    filtered[t, ] <- prob

    # accumulate the log likelihood
    # scaling at each step helps avoid numerical underflow
    loglik <- loglik + log(scale)
  }

  list(loglik = loglik, filtered = filtered)
}

# function to find the most likely complete hidden state sequence
viterbi_hmm <- function(emission, Gamma, delta) {
  n <- nrow(emission)
  k <- ncol(emission)

  # store the best log score and previous state for each position
  score <- matrix(-Inf, n, k)
  previous <- matrix(0L, n, k)

  # initialise using the first observation and initial probabilities
  score[1, ] <- log(delta) + log(emission[1, ])

  if (n > 1) {
    for (t in 2:n) {
      for (j in seq_len(k)) {

        # compare paths entering state j from each possible previous state
        candidate <- score[t - 1, ] + log(Gamma[, j])

        # save the best previous state and update the path score
        previous[t, j] <- which.max(candidate)
        score[t, j] <- max(candidate) + log(emission[t, j])
      }
    }
  }

  # start with the best final state
  path <- integer(n)
  path[n] <- which.max(score[n, ])

  # work backwards to recover the most likely state sequence
  if (n > 1) {
    for (t in seq.int(n - 1, 1)) {
      path[t] <- previous[t + 1, path[t + 1]]
    }
  }

  path
}
```


## Question 1

### 1. Simulate 20 observations from the following three-state HMM. All three state distributions are two-dimensional Gaussian (Figure 5 in the notes):

   $$
   [\mathbf{x}_t \mid z_t = k, \theta]
   \sim N(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \Sigma_k)
   $$

   with transition probability matrix

   $$
   \Gamma =
   \begin{pmatrix}
   0.8 & 0.1 & 0.1 \\
   0.1 & 0.8 & 0.1 \\
   0.1 & 0.1 & 0.8
   \end{pmatrix}.
   $$

```{r}
# mean vectors for the three states
mu <- 10 * matrix(
  c(-1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1),
  ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE
)

# covariance matrices for the three states
sf <- 10
sigma <- array(0, dim = c(2, 2, 3))

sigma[, , 1] <- sf * matrix(c(1, 1/2, 1/2, 1), nrow = 2)
sigma[, , 2] <- sf * matrix(c(1, -1/2, -1/2, 1), nrow = 2)
sigma[, , 3] <- sf * matrix(c(3, 0, 0, 1/2), nrow = 2)

# transition probabilities between states
Gamma <- matrix(
  c(0.8, 0.1, 0.1,
    0.1, 0.8, 0.1,
    0.1, 0.1, 0.8),
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE
)

# simulate the hidden states using a stationary initial distribution
set.seed(4010)
n <- 20
delta <- stationary(Gamma)
states <- simulate_states(n, Gamma, delta)

# generate each observation using its state's mean and covariance
observations <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = 2)

for (t in seq_len(n)) {
  k <- states[t]

  observations[t, ] <- mu[k, ] +
    drop(t(chol(sigma[, , k])) %*% rnorm(2))
}

# combine the observations and true states
simulated_data <- data.frame(
  time = seq_len(n),
  x1 = observations[, 1],
  x2 = observations[, 2],
  state = factor(states, levels = 1:3)
)

simulated_data
```


I first simulated 20 hidden states using the transition matrix and its stationary distribution, which assigns probability \(1/3\) to each initial state. The probability of remaining in the current state is 0.8, while the total probability of switching is 0.2, so runs within the same state are expected. Each observation was then generated from the bivariate Gaussian distribution associated with its state. The code selects the appropriate mean vector and covariance matrix using `states[t]`. Observations from the same state still differ because they are random draws from that distribution.


### 2. Plot the observations $Y_t$, colour-coded by their true state. Also indicate the path of these observations, as this is a time series.

```{r}
# plot the observations and connect them in time order
ggplot(simulated_data, aes(x1, x2)) +
  geom_path(
    aes(group = 1),
    colour = "grey60",
    arrow = grid::arrow(
      length = grid::unit(0.1, "inches")
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = state), size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = time), nudge_y = 0.8, size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("1" = "blue", "2" = "red", "3" = "darkgreen"),
    drop = FALSE
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    x = "First component",
    y = "Second component",
    colour = "True state"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

The plot shows three distinct groups corresponding to the hidden states. State 1 observations (blue) lie on the left, state 2 observations (red) on the lower right, and state 3 observations (green) towards the top. These locations are consistent with the specified mean vectors \((-10,0)\), \((10,0)\) and \((0,10)\).

The numbered points and connecting lines show the sequence over time. Observations 1–7 remain in state 2, while observations 12–17 remain in state 3, illustrating the persistence encouraged by the 0.8 probability of staying in the current state. Other points show switches between states. Variation within each group reflects the randomness of the Gaussian observations and their state-specific covariance matrices.

### 3. If you had to estimate the parameters for this situation, given only the observations, what are the parameters, and how many are there?

If only the observations were available and all model parameters were unknown, I would estimate the transition probabilities and the mean vector and covariance matrix for each of the three states. Each transition matrix row has two free probabilities because its three entries must sum to one, giving $(3(3-1)=6$ free parameters. Each bivariate Gaussian distribution has two means and three distinct covariance parameters, giving $3(2+3)=15$ parameters across the states. The total is therefore $6+15=21$ free parameters when the initial distribution is determined by stationarity. If the initial distribution is estimated separately, it contributes two additional free parameters, giving 23. The hidden state sequence is inferred separately and is not included in this parameter count.

## Question 2

The following are 10 observations from a three-state HMM, with states A, B and C, and possible observations x, y and z:

```{r}
obs <- c("x", "x", "x", "x", "x", "x", "x", "z", "z", "y")
```

Use the following initial state probabilities, transition probability matrix and emission probability matrix:

```{r}
init <- c(0.4, 0.3, 0.3)

tpm <- matrix(
  c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2,
    0.1, 0.6, 0.3,
    0.2, 0.2, 0.6),
  byrow = TRUE, ncol = 3
)

emmprob <- matrix(
  c(0.6, 0.2, 0.2,
    0.1, 0.5, 0.4,
    0.3, 0.3, 0.4),
  byrow = TRUE, ncol = 3
)
```

### 1. Use the Viterbi algorithm to find the most likely state sequence, given the observations.

```{r}
# observations and possible states
obs <- c(rep("x", 7), "z", "z", "y")
obsposs <- c("x", "y", "z")
state_names <- c("A", "B", "C")

# initial state probabilities
init <- c(0.4, 0.3, 0.3)

# transition probabilities, rows are current states
tpm <- matrix(
  c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2,
    0.1, 0.6, 0.3,
    0.2, 0.2, 0.6),
  byrow = TRUE, ncol = 3
)

# emission probabilities, rows are states and columns are x, y, z
emmprob <- matrix(
  c(0.6, 0.2, 0.2,
    0.1, 0.5, 0.4,
    0.3, 0.3, 0.4),
  byrow = TRUE, ncol = 3
)

# use log probabilities to avoid multiplying small numbers
log_init <- log2(init)
Gamma <- log2(tpm)
em.probs <- log2(emmprob)

n <- length(obs)
K <- length(state_names)

# store the best log score for each state at each time
xi <- matrix(0, nrow = K, ncol = n)

# initialise using the first observation
oi <- match(obs[1], obsposs)
xi[, 1] <- log_init + em.probs[, oi]

# calculate the best path score ending in each state
for (i in 2:n) {
  oi <- match(obs[i], obsposs)

  for (j in seq_len(K)) {
    xi[j, i] <- max(xi[, i - 1] + Gamma[, j]) +
      em.probs[j, oi]
  }
}

# backtrack from the best final state
path <- integer(n)
path[n] <- which.max(xi[, n])

for (i in seq.int(n - 1, 1)) {
  path[i] <- which.max(xi[, i] + Gamma[, path[i + 1]])
}

# compare the decoded and true states
decoded <- state_names[path]
true_states <- c("A", "C", "A", "A", "A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B")

comparison <- data.frame(
  time = seq_len(n),
  observation = obs,
  true_state = true_states,
  decoded_state = decoded
)

decoded
```


### 2. Briefly explain and illustrate your results.
```{r}
# combine the true and decoded sequences for plotting
plot_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    time = seq_len(n),
    state = match(true_states, state_names),
    sequence = "True"
  ),
  data.frame(
    time = seq_len(n),
    state = path,
    sequence = "Viterbi"
  )
)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(time, state, colour = sequence)) +
  geom_step() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq_len(n)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:3, labels = state_names) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("True" = "black", "Viterbi" = "blue")) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "State", colour = NULL) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The Viterbi algorithm assigns state A to the first seven observations and state B to the final three. This is consistent with the emission probabilities, since A has the highest probability of producing `x`, while B can produce `z` and has the highest probability of producing `y`. The algorithm also accounts for transition probabilities when selecting the most likely complete sequence.

The decoded sequence agrees with the true sequence except at time 2, where it selects A instead of C. Although C can produce `x`, remaining in A gives a more probable overall path than switching to C and then returning to A. This illustrates that the most likely state sequence does not necessarily recover every true hidden state.


## Question 3
Consider a stationary two-state Poisson HMM with parameters

$$
\Gamma =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.1 & 0.9 \\
0.4 & 0.6
\end{pmatrix}
$$

and $\lambda=(1,3)$.

In each of the following ways, compute the probability that the first three observations are $0,2,1$.

### 1. Consider all possible sequences of states of the Markov chain that could have occurred. Compute the probability of each sequence and the probability of the observations given each sequence.

```{r}
# transition probabilities and state-specific Poisson means
Gamma3 <- matrix(
  c(0.1, 0.9,
    0.4, 0.6),
  nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE
)

lambda3 <- c(1, 3)
x3 <- c(0, 2, 1)

# stationary initial probabilities
delta3 <- stationary(Gamma3)
delta3

# list all eight possible hidden state sequences
paths3 <- expand.grid(
  s1 = 1:2,
  s2 = 1:2,
  s3 = 1:2
)

# probability of each hidden state sequence
paths3$state_probability <- apply(paths3[, 1:3], 1, function(s) {
  delta3[s[1]] *
    Gamma3[s[1], s[2]] *
    Gamma3[s[2], s[3]]
})

# probability of observing 0, 2, 1 given each state sequence
paths3$observation_given_states <- apply(
  paths3[, 1:3], 1, function(s) {
    prod(dpois(x3, lambda = lambda3[s]))
  }
)

# joint probability of each state sequence and the observations
paths3$joint_probability <-
  paths3$state_probability * paths3$observation_given_states

paths3

# sum over all possible hidden state sequences
probability_a <- sum(paths3$joint_probability)
probability_a
```

### 2. Apply the formula

```{r}
# diagonal matrix of observation probabilities under each state
P3 <- function(x) {
  diag(dpois(x, lambda = lambda3))
}

# sum over the hidden states through matrix multiplication
probability_b <- drop(
  delta3 %*% P3(0) %*%
    Gamma3 %*% P3(2) %*%
    Gamma3 %*% P3(1) %*%
    rep(1, 2)
)

# compare the two methods
c(enumeration = probability_a, matrix = probability_b)
```

## Question 4

We have the general expression

$$
L_T=\delta P(x_1)\Gamma P(x_2)\cdots\Gamma P(x_T)\mathbf{1}
$$

for the likelihood of an HMM, for example of Poisson type. Consider the special case in which the Markov chain becomes a sequence of independent random variables, giving an independent mixture model.

Show that the likelihood simplifies to

$$
L_T(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m,\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_m)
=
\prod_{j=1}^{T}
\left[
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_i p_i(x_j;\theta_i)
\right].
$$


## Question 6: The occasionally dishonest casino

Use the probabilities shown in the source diagram. The initial distribution and simulation length were not specified; use stationarity and 500 rolls.

```{r}
# transition probabilities, states are fair and loaded
Gamma6 <- matrix(
  c(0.95, 0.05,
    0.10, 0.90),
  nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE
)

# outcome probabilities for each die
emission6 <- rbind(
  Fair = rep(1/6, 6),
  Loaded = c(rep(0.1, 5), 0.5)
)

# simulate the hidden die sequence
set.seed(4010)
n6 <- 500
delta6 <- stationary(Gamma6)
states6 <- simulate_states(n6, Gamma6, delta6)

# simulate each roll using the selected die
rolls6 <- integer(n6)

for (t in seq_len(n6)) {
  rolls6[t] <- sample(
    1:6, size = 1,
    prob = emission6[states6[t], ]
  )
}

# combine the rolls and true states
casino_data <- data.frame(
  time = seq_len(n6),
  roll = rolls6,
  state = factor(
    states6,
    levels = 1:2,
    labels = c("Fair", "Loaded")
  )
)

# plot the simulated outcomes
ggplot(casino_data, aes(time, roll, colour = state)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:6) +
  labs(
    x = "Roll number",
    y = "Die outcome",
    colour = "True state"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

# compare outcome proportions within each state
prop.table(table(casino_data$state, casino_data$roll), margin = 1)
```



## Question 7: Two-state Bernoulli HMM

Assume a two-state Bernoulli HMM defined as follows.

The transition probability matrix is

$$
\Gamma =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.5 & 0.5 \\
0.25 & 0.75
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The state-dependent distributions are given by

$$
P(X_t=x \mid C_t=1)=0.5,
\qquad x=0,1,
$$

and

$$
P(X_t=1 \mid C_t=2)=1.
$$

The stationary distribution is

$$
\delta=\frac{1}{3}(1,2).
$$

Find $P(0)$ and $P(1)$.

Write a function to calculate the likelihood.

Check that, for the observations $(X_1=1,X_2=1,X_3=1)$,

$$
L=\frac{29}{48}.
$$
```{r}
# transition probabilities
Gamma7 <- matrix(
  c(0.5, 0.5,
    0.25, 0.75),
  nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE
)

# stationary initial distribution
delta7 <- c(1/3, 2/3)

# probability of observing 1 in each state
p7 <- c(0.5, 1)

# diagonal matrices of observation probabilities
P7 <- function(x) {
  diag(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = p7))
}

P7(0)
P7(1)

# function to calculate the Bernoulli HMM likelihood
bernoulli_likelihood <- function(x, log = FALSE) {
  stopifnot(length(x) > 0, all(x %in% c(0, 1)))

  phi <- delta7
  ll <- 0

  for (i in seq_along(x)) {
    Pi <- P7(x[i])

    # use the initial distribution for the first observation
    # and transition probabilities for subsequent observations
    if (i == 1) {
      v <- phi %*% Pi
    } else {
      v <- phi %*% Gamma7 %*% Pi
    }

    # normalise and accumulate the log likelihood
    u <- sum(v)

    if (u <= 0) {
      return(if (log) -Inf else 0)
    }

    ll <- ll + log(u)
    phi <- drop(v / u)
  }

  if (log) ll else exp(ll)
}

# check against the supplied answer
c(
  calculated = bernoulli_likelihood(c(1, 1, 1)),
  expected = 29/48
)
```

# Reflection
This tutorial helped me consolidate my understanding of Hidden Markov Models and how an unobserved state sequence influences the observations. I explored simulation, transition and emission probabilities, Viterbi decoding, and likelihood calculations. Adapting the lecture code helped me connect the mathematical expressions to their implementation in R. I also learned that finding the most likely state sequence differs from calculating the likelihood, which sums over all possible hidden paths.

Due to time constraints, I decided not to complete Questions 5 and 8. My next steps are to revisit these questions, practise explaining the forward and Viterbi algorithms in my own words, and strengthen my understanding of how HMM parameters are estimated.
